title: Celestial Writing (Scriptura coelestis)
otherNames: Angelic script / Angelic alphabet (modern websites, e.g. Omniglot; not Agrippa's name for it)
family: Hebrew-based ring-letter (charaktêres / 'Brillenbuchstaben') alphabets: sister of Malachim and Transitus fluvii (Passing the River)
summary: The Celestial Writing is a 22-letter alphabet, one sign for each Hebrew letter, drawn in thin strokes; modern charts show small rings at the stroke-ends. Agrippa printed it in De occulta philosophia, Book III, chapter 30, in the first complete edition ([Cologne], colophon July 1533), with the Malachim and Passing the River. He does not claim it as his own. He reports that the Hebrews call it 'celestial' because they show it set and figured among the stars, as astrologers draw the images of the signs from the outlines ('lineaments') of the stars. In that chapter he gives it no rite or use. It reached English readers in the J.F. translation (London, 1651, p. 439) and in Francis Barrett's The Magus (London, 1801).

firstAttestation.author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
firstAttestation.place: [Cologne]. The printer is usually given as Johannes Soter; Eton College's catalogue records the attribution with a query and notes Adams's suggestion of Basel. Catalogues report four or five issues dated 1533.
firstAttestation.locator: Book III, chapter 30. The 1651 English heading, verified in EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789), is 'CHAP. XXX. Another manner of making Characters, delivered by Cabalists.' In 1651 the 'Celestiall writing' table is on p. 439, at the head of the chapter; Malachim follows on p. 440 and 'the passing of the River' on p. 441. For 1533, the Celestial is reported as the top row of a single figure of three alphabets (a stock-image caption cited in the Malachim research file); this was not seen. The 1533 page or signature is unverified. Wikipedia, as reported in the Transitus fluvii file, gives p. 491 of Perrone Compagni's 1992 edition; this was not checked.
firstAttestation.notes: This is the earliest printing of this alphabet that has been documented. Agrippa sent a manuscript draft of the work to Trithemius, abbot of St Jakob, Würzburg. Trithemius's reply, printed in the front matter of the 1651 English, is dated 'From our Monastery of Peapolis, the 8. day of April, An. M. D. X.' (EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789)), so the draft had reached him by 8 April 1510. Whether that draft already contained this chapter and its tables has not been checked; Perrone Compagni's critical edition (Brill, 1992) would settle it. OPEN LEAD: the Malachim research file reports a claim (Cipher Mysteries blog, 2009) that the 'transitus fluvii' alphabet in Pantheus's Voarchadumia (Venice, 1530) is 'a conglomeration of all three of Agrippa's alphabets'. If Celestial-like signs are on that plate, the Celestial was in print three years before 1533. This is unverified. Websites that date the Celestial to 1531 are confusing it with the 1531 printings, which contained Book I only.

transmission.work: De occulta philosophia (manuscript draft dedicated to Trithemius)
transmission.author: Agrippa
transmission.what: The early draft of the work. Trithemius's reply acknowledging it is dated 8 April 1510 (1651 English front matter, EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789)). Whether the draft contained the chapter of Hebrew alphabets is unverified.

transmission.work: Miqneh Avram / Peculium Abrae (Venice: Daniel Bomberg)
transmission.author: Abraham de Balmes
transmission.what: Context, not the Celestial itself. This grammar prints a ring-letter alphabet called Ketav ever ha-nahar ('script beyond the river') as an example of derivative alphabets. Macfarlane calls it the first printed alphabet of this kind. It is the ancestor of Agrippa's Passing the River.

transmission.work: De occulta philosophia libri tres, III.30 ([Cologne: J. Soter?])
transmission.author: Agrippa
transmission.what: The first documented printing of the Scriptura coelestis. It is reported as the top row of a woodcut naming the Hebrew letters, above the Malachim and Transitus fluvii rows (stock-image caption; not seen). One sentence explains the name.

transmission.work: De originibus seu de Hebraicae linguae et gentis antiquitate (Paris)
transmission.author: Guillaume Postel
transmission.what: A parallel idea, not this alphabet. Only a bookseller's description (Peter Harrington, on Gaffarel 1629) credits Postel with first arguing that the Hebrew letters can be read in the constellations. The work and the passage were not checked.

transmission.author: Agrippa
transmission.what: Reported as a later Latin printing with the passage and the alphabet tables. Travis Shores reproduces the three alphabets from a '1550 reprint', and the Source Library site is reported to host a '1550' copy of the passage. The date of this edition was not confirmed. Its woodcuts would be re-cut, so its forms may differ from 1533; they have not been compared.

transmission.work: Thrésor de l'histoire des langues de cest univers (Cologny: Matthieu Berjon; posthumous)
transmission.author: Claude Duret (d. 1611)
transmission.what: Reported to reprint a 'Scriptura Celestis'. Peterson is reported to cite it at p. 119, giving the place as 'Cologne'. The page was not checked against a scan, and the Transitus fluvii researcher could not confirm that Duret prints the sister alphabet.

transmission.work: Curiositez inouyes sur la sculpture talismanique des Persans, horoscope des Patriarches, et lecture des estoilles (Paris)
transmission.author: Jacques Gaffarel
transmission.what: A different 'celestial writing'. It has two folding planispheres on which the constellations themselves form Hebrew letters, which Gaffarel credits to a 'R. Chomer'. It gave Agrippa's one-line etymology a full theory. English translation by Edmund Chilmead, Unheard-of Curiosities (London: Humphrey Moseley, 1650).

transmission.work: Three Books of Occult Philosophy (London: Printed by R.W. for Gregory Moule, 1651; Wing A789)
transmission.author: Agrippa, translated by 'J.F.' (the EEBO-TCP record, from the Harvard copy, says 'The translator is probably John French', 1616-1657)
transmission.what: English translation of III.30, verified in EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789). The 'Celestiall writing.' table is on p. 439. It is laid out in three rows of 7, 7 and 8 letter-names, and the names run right to left: row 1 reads 'Zain Vau He Daleth Gimel Beth Aleph', so Aleph stands at the right. The table prints names only, with no numbers and no final forms. The glyphs themselves are not transcribed (TCP marks them 'in non-Latin alphabet').

transmission.author: Thomas Bang (Bangius)
transmission.what: A study of letters and their origins. Macfarlane treats it as a learned response to two things: the Enoch fragments and the idea of celestial writing (above all Gaffarel's) as threats to Christian teaching on angels. The snippets I read characterise Bang's stance in conflicting ways.

transmission.work: The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer (London: Lackington, Allen & Co.)
transmission.author: Francis Barrett
transmission.what: Reported to copy Agrippa's text in Book II, Part I, chapter XVI, as given by the sacred-texts transcription; the chapter and heading were not re-checked. A plate is reported (Source Library) with four registers: Theban, Celestial Writing, Malachim, Passing the River. Its plate number was not verified. Many modern charts appear to follow it.

transmission.author: Joseph H. Peterson
transmission.what: Reported to publish a 'Celestial writing' font taken from De occulta philosophia III (1533), with a CC-BY 4.0 licence stated on the fonts page. The page was not re-checked.

transmission.work: 'Written in the Stars? Alphabets and Angels in Early Modern Europe', Journal of the History of Ideas 86.3, pp. 473-506
transmission.author: Kirsten Macfarlane
transmission.what: The scholarly account, as described in its abstract and snippets, of how Christian scholars came to treat Brillenbuchstaben from medieval Jewish kabbalistic manuscripts as alphabets derived from the stars and written by angels. The bibliographic details were not re-verified.

claims.claim: The Hebrews call this writing 'celestial' because they show it placed and figured among the stars, just as astrologers draw the images of the signs from the lines of the stars.
claims.evidence: This is documented only as Agrippa's report. The 1651 English (verified in EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789)) reads: 'There is also amongst them a writing which they call Celestiall, because they shew it placed and figured amongst the Stars, no otherwise then the other Astrologers produce images of signs from the lineaments of Stars.' The Latin was not seen. Agrippa reports that the letters come from star-figures; he does not demonstrate it.
sources: J.F. trans. 1651, Book III ch. XXX, p. 439 (EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789), verified)

claims.claim: The letters are formed from the figures of the stars.
claims.evidence: Agrippa's sentence is the only basis for this. Gaffarel (1629) later built it into a theory. A bookseller's description credits Postel (1538) with the idea earlier, which is unverified. No source found shows that any Celestial letter matches a real constellation.
sources: Peter Harrington catalogue on Gaffarel 1629 (bookseller; for Postel 1538)

claims.evidence: Wikipedia and Omniglot say 'created by Agrippa'. Agrippa himself presents it as a writing found 'amongst them', the Hebrews (1651 English, verified; the Latin was not seen). Macfarlane places ring-ended letters of this kind in medieval Jewish kabbalistic manuscripts. No copy of this specific alphabet earlier than 1533 has been confirmed, but see the unverified Pantheus 1530 lead. Its maker is unknown.

claims.claim: The Celestial alphabet was made to communicate with angels.
claims.evidence: This is a modern website claim (Wikipedia, Omniglot) with no early source. In III.30 Agrippa glosses only the Malachim as 'of Angels, or Regal' (1651 English, verified), and he assigns no use to the Celestial. The angelic reading of these scripts belongs to later learned readers (Macfarlane) and to the name 'Malachim'.

claims.claim: Its ring-ended strokes belong to the charaktêres tradition.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation, not a stated derivation. Bohak (2011) traces ring-ended charaktêres to Graeco-Egyptian magic and shows they are central to Jewish magical texts from Late Antiquity on. The Rylands posts are reported to describe them as signs of angelic scripts. Linking Agrippa's Celestial to this family rests on graphic resemblance and on Macfarlane's framing.
The 1531 printings (Paris, Antwerp, Cologne) contained Book I only. Book III, and with it chapter 30, first appeared in the complete edition of 1533.
sources: Wellcome and Eton catalogue records of the 1533 edition

claims.claim: It is the same as Dee and Kelley's 'Enochian' or 'celestial' alphabet.
claims.evidence: It is not. Enochian (1580s) is a separate alphabet that is sometimes also called 'celestial' or 'angelic'. Wikipedia warns against the confusion.

claims.claim: Grimoires wrote angel names in this alphabet on pentacles.
claims.evidence: This is documented for the sister scripts in Mathers's Key of Solomon (1889): Malachim around a pentacle of Mars and in a conjuration, and Passing the River in the Plate III pentacle. My searches found no grimoire passage that uses the Celestial specifically.
sources: Mathers, Key of Solomon (Esoteric Archives; sacred-texts Plate III)

letters.name: Aleph
letters.form: UNVERIFIED RECONSTRUCTION HINT, NOT AGRIPPA'S FORM AS SEEN. Neither the researcher nor the fact-checker could view the 1533 woodcut, the 1651 table or any reproduction. This gives the skeleton of the Hebrew square letter that the Celestial letter is reported to resemble, in thin strokes, with a small ring at the free stroke-ends. Whether each ring is open or filled, and which ends carry one, must be taken from the source plate. Skeleton: one long diagonal from upper left to lower right; a short upper-right arm that drops from the top right and meets the upper half of the diagonal; a short lower-left leg that rises from the bottom left to meet the lower half. Three free tips.
letters.note: 1651 label: 'Aleph' (EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789), p. 439). Value and order follow the Hebrew alphabet, as the table keys it. The numeric value is the standard Hebrew one; the 1651 table prints names only, with no numbers. FACT-CHECK OF FORM: The Hebrew skeleton is described correctly, except that the upper arm meets the diagonal in its upper half rather than at its middle (fixed). With three free tips, ring placement is a guess. The Agrippa form has not been confirmed. Trace the glyph from the 1533 woodcut (Library of Congress digitised copy; link to be re-verified), from the 1651 table (EEBO page image tcp:52070:235), or from Peterson's 1533-based 'Celestial writing' font (licence to be confirmed).

lettersSource: Order, names and values: 22 letters keyed one-for-one to the Hebrew alphabet, in Hebrew order. The names follow the labels of the 1651 'Celestiall writing.' table (EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789), p. 439): Aleph, Beth, Gimel, Daleth, He, Vau, Zain, Cheth, Theth, Iod, Caph, Lamed, Mem, Nun, Samech, Ain, Pe, Zade, Kuff, Res, Shin, Tau. That table has 22 names, no final forms and no numbers. It is set in three rows of 7, 7 and 8 names running right to left, with Aleph at the right of row 1. The 1533 labels and layout were not seen. FORMS: NONE VERIFIED. No image or facsimile could be viewed by the researcher or the fact-checker, and no text found describes the glyphs letter by letter. Each 'form' is a low-confidence hint: the Hebrew square-letter skeleton with rings at the free ends. Its basis is a report (an encoding draft) that most Celestial letters resemble their Hebrew counterparts. To draw the letters, trace the 1533 woodcut (III.30; Library of Congress digitised copy, link to be re-verified), the 1651 table (p. 439; EEBO page image tcp:52070:235), or Peterson's 'Celestial writing' font, which he is reported to have taken from 1533. Name the source used. Do not use Barrett's 1801 plate as the model.

uses.use: Displayed in Agrippa as one of the Hebrew 'fashions of characters'
uses.evidence: III.30 (1651 English, verified) first names the most ancient script, which Moses and the prophets used and whose form 'is not rashly to be discovered to any', and notes that the letters in use today were instituted by Esdras. It then names the Celestial, the Malachim and 'the passing through the River', and prints the three tables (pp. 439-441 in 1651). The chapter then turns to the Cabalists' 'nine Chambers' method of making characters. No rite is attached to the Celestial.

uses.use: Context of characters for spirits and angels in Book III
uses.evidence: It sits between III.29, 'Of the Characters and Seals of spirits', where Agrippa gives the Theban letters as those 'which Peter Apponus notes, as delivered by Honorius of Thebes', and III.31, 'There is yet another fashion of Characters, and concerning marks of spirits which are received only by revelation' (1651 headings, verified in EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789)). This setting among chapters on spirit characters is the context for the later association of these scripts with angels (Macfarlane 2025). No specific use of the Celestial for angel names was found.

uses.use: Learned discussion of the origin of letters
uses.evidence: Duret (1613) reprints it in a history of languages. Gaffarel (1629) develops star-writing into a theory. Bang (1657) responds to the idea of celestial writing (Macfarlane 2025).

uses.use: Writing angel names on pentacles and talismans
uses.evidence: Not documented for the Celestial in the sources I found. Mathers's Key of Solomon (1889) uses Malachim and Passing the River for this. If the site mentions the practice, it should say it is attested for the sister scripts.

uses.use: Modern substitution cipher, decoration and font
uses.evidence: dCode and Omniglot present it as a letter-for-letter substitution for Hebrew, and also apply it to Latin-letter text. Peterson's font dates from 2016. A 20th-century drawing of the alphabet, with notes naming Postel and Agrippa, is reported in the Museum of Witchcraft and Magic archive (R/6/859); not re-checked.

Sister alphabet printed with it in III.30. It is reported as the next row of the same 1533 woodcut; in 1651 it is a separate table on p. 440.
Sister alphabet in III.30; descends from de Balmes's Ketav ever ha-nahar (Venice, 1523).
Printed in the preceding chapter, III.29 (1651 heading verified). Barrett's 1801 plate is reported to set Theban above the Celestial.
On Bohak's account (2011), ring-ended charaktêres arose in Graeco-Egyptian magic and passed into Jewish magic. The Celestial's link to them is one of graphic resemblance, not a documented derivation.
The word charaktêr, 'engraved mark', is Greek.

cautions: LETTER FORMS ARE UNVERIFIED. Every 'form' is a reconstruction hint based on the Hebrew skeleton. Neither the researcher nor the fact-checker saw any image. Drawing them as 'Agrippa's Celestial' without tracing the 1533 woodcut, the 1651 p. 439 table or Peterson's 1533-based font would present guesses as the source.

The chapter number and heading are now verified for 1651 (EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789)): 'CHAP. XXX. Another manner of making Characters, delivered by Cabalists.', p. 439. Do not use 'delivered by Angels', and do not cite the passage as III.28.
Do not date it 1531: Book III first appeared in 1533.
Do not call it 'invented by Agrippa', and do not say it was 'used to talk with angels'. Agrippa reports it as a Hebrew script and gives it no use.

Keep it apart from three other things: Dee and Kelley's Enochian (also called 'celestial' or 'angelic'), Gaffarel's 1629 constellation-letters (a different 'celestial writing'), and the star-letter idea a bookseller credits to Postel (1538, unverified).
Later printings re-cut the table (1651, Barrett 1801; Duret 1613 and the '1550' Latin edition are reported), so forms may drift between editions. The page should name the edition it follows.
Peterson is reported to give Duret's imprint as 'Cologne, 1613'. Library catalogues give Cologny (near Geneva), 1613, a posthumous edition; Duret died in 1611.
The printer of the 1533 edition is usually given as Johannes Soter of Cologne, but some catalogues query it (Adams is reported to suggest Basel).

Layout and direction: in 1651 the table runs right to left, with Aleph at the right of the first of three rows (EEBO-TCP A26565 (Wing A789)). That is the layout of a printed table and does not prove a writing direction. Wikipedia (left to right) and dCode (right to left) disagree, and the 1533 layout was not seen.
Ring-ends: whether rings are open or filled, and which stroke-ends carry them, must be taken from the chosen source plate. No source in this file describes them.
Peterson's transcriptions carry a copyright notice. His fonts page is reported to state CC-BY 4.0; confirm the licence for the Celestial font on the page before embedding it, and credit it.
Pages and folios: the 1651 page (p. 439) is verified. The 1533 page or signature, Perrone Compagni p. 491, Duret p. 119, and Barrett's chapter and plate placement are not.

Translator: do not write 'John Freake'. The EEBO-TCP/Harvard record says 'probably John French'. Donald Tyson's 1993 Llewellyn edition credits 'James Freake' (the fact-checker's recollection, not re-verified). If the page names anyone, give 'J.F.' and say the identification is uncertain.

confidence: SOLID: the alphabet is printed in Agrippa's De occulta philosophia III.30 in the complete edition of 1533, with the Malachim and Transitus fluvii. The 1651 English is verified against EEBO-TCP A26565: the chapter number and heading ('Another manner of making Characters, delivered by Cabalists'), Agrippa's one-sentence explanation of the name, the table on p. 439, its 22 names in Hebrew order with no numbers or final forms, and its right-to-left three-row layout. Trithemius's reply to the 1510 draft is dated 8 April 1510. REPORTED, NOT RE-VERIFIED: Barrett's chapter (Book II, Part I, ch. XVI) and plate; Macfarlane's 2025 framing and its bibliographic details; Bohak 2011; the Rylands posts; Duret's p. 119; Peterson's font and its licence; the '1550' Latin edition; Bang's stance. SHAKY OR ABSENT: every letter form (none seen; all 22 are low-confidence hints); the 1533 page, layout and Latin wording; whether the 1510 draft has the chapter; the Pantheus 1530 lead; the Postel 1538 attribution (a bookseller only). No use of the Celestial specifically on talismans has been found; such use is attested only for its sister scripts. Most source URLs were withdrawn pending re-verification.
